slides.title: A Local AI Developer Stack, Measured
slides.subtitle: Surface Laptop Ultra with NVIDIA RTX Spark: code generation, doc RAG, hybrid routing
slides.notes: Today is architecture and measured numbers, not marketing. We'll show how a Surface Laptop Ultra with NVIDIA RTX Spark runs a local developer stack: code generation, retrieval over internal docs, and hybrid routing to cloud for the heaviest reasoning. We close with one ask: a 10-developer, 2-week technical pilot.

slides.notes: Read bottom-up. The NVIDIA RTX Spark N1X pairs a Blackwell RTX GPU with 20 CPU cores. llama.cpp build 11573 runs native ARM64 with CUDA; Foundry Local uses the CUDA execution provider. The local catalog holds 28 open models, 315 GiB on disk. Developer workflows sit on top.

slides.title: Three Memory Views, Never Summed
slides.takeaway: Installed, Windows-visible and GPU-budget figures are distinct views; never add them.
slides.notes: Think of three maps of one city: you never add the maps together. 128 GB is installed. Windows reports about 64 GB visible. nvidia-smi reports a 64,000 MiB GPU memory budget. These are distinct views of memory, not slices to sum. When anyone asks how much memory, the honest answer starts with: which view?

slides.title: Measured Throughput, Single and Concurrent
slides.takeaway: Qwen3-Coder: first token in 0.13 s; aggregate throughput rises with concurrency.

data.caption: Local-AI-Bench, this device, Oct 2026, shared machine

slides.notes: All figures: Local-AI-Bench on this device, October 2026, shared machine, so treat them as measurements, not guaranteed specs. Qwen3-Coder 30B: about 86 tokens/s single stream, 0.13 s to first token, about 140 aggregate across 4 streams. Gemma 4 26B: about 72 single, about 245 across 8. Concurrency matters when agents run parallel requests.

slides.title: Why MoE Decodes Several Times Faster
slides.takeaway: Similar size, less work per token: MoE activates only a few experts.

data.verdict: MoE decodes several times faster at similar size.

slides.notes: Two models of similar size, one measured difference. Dense Qwen3.6 27B pushes every token through all its weights: about 13 tokens per second. Qwen3-Coder 30B is a mixture of experts with about 3B parameters active per token: about 86 tokens per second. Same laptop, same benchmark. Speed is not accuracy; pilot acceptance rates will tell us that.

slides.title: MoE Works Like a Specialist Team
slides.takeaway: All experts stay loaded; only a few work on each token.
slides.notes: Picture a specialist engineering team. Everyone is on the roster, but each task goes only to the few specialists it needs. Qwen3-Coder 30B works the same way: about 3B parameters activate per token. A dense model calls the whole team into every meeting. Note the trade: the full model still loads into memory; compute per token shrinks.

slides.title: Size Models Like Shop Machines
slides.takeaway: Bands are planning estimates, not accuracy tiers; pick the band that fits.
slides.notes: Zava already thinks this way on the shop floor: pick the machine whose envelope fits the job, and nobody assumes the gantry mill is more precise. Model bands work the same: S 1-4B, M 7-8B, L 14-20B, XL 24-32B parameters. Planning estimates, not accuracy tiers. Qwen3-Coder 30B is XL, yet MoE keeps it fast.

slides.notes: This is the developer loop. A question starts in the IDE. Retrieval searches Zava's internal engineering docs and code locally, and the best passages ground the prompt. Qwen3-Coder 30B generates on the laptop through llama.cpp. The developer accepts, edits or rejects, and the pilot logs acceptance. Sensitive source and doc context stays in this local lane.

slides.title: Hybrid Routing: Sensitive Work Stays Local
slides.takeaway: Sensitive, frequent tasks stay local; the heaviest reasoning can route to cloud.
slides.notes: Every request hits a routing policy first. Sensitive, frequent work, meaning code and internal docs, stays in the local lane: Qwen3-Coder, local doc retrieval, llama.cpp and Foundry Local. The heaviest reasoning can route to cloud models by policy. Think in-house machine shop for sensitive parts, outside foundry for the biggest castings.

slides.title: A Two-Week Pilot, Measured End to End
slides.takeaway: 10 developers, 14 days, measuring acceptance rate, latency and developer experience.
slides.notes: Ten developers, fourteen days. Start: install the stack and index a scoped set of internal docs. Week one: code generation inside daily work. Week two: add doc retrieval and hybrid routing. Day 14: we read out acceptance rate, latency and developer experience, measured on Zava's real work, not a benchmark.
